title: Marginal Operation
label: Quick read (from summaries)
premise: Arata, a thirty-year-old former NEET who has lost his job, signs on with a private military company and turns out to be gifted as an 'operator' who directs soldiers remotely, first in Central Asia (J-Novel Club blurb; ANN). Disgusted that his employer uses a unit of child soldiers as bait, he takes responsibility for the children and eventually founds his own security company staffed by them, trying to secure them a future through the only skill he has (AniList user review; MangaUpdates tags). A 16-volume seinen adaptation of Yuri Shibamura's novels.
life_message: It holds up fierce, practical devotion to the vulnerable people in your care, even when every option left is morally compromised.

content.note: Military combat, terrorism and guns throughout (AniList tags; MangaUpdates 'Violence', 'Blood and Gore', 'Murder/s'); children fight as soldiers (MangaUpdates; AniList review).
Kidnapping, war zones and children at mortal risk; review notes real psychological costs.

Non-explicit: a sex-worker character appears (ANN); MangaUpdates tags prostitution and rape; review says rescued slum children otherwise faced sexual exploitation. Adult protagonist with a slow romance.
Military setting; profanity likely but not described (to verify).
Isolation, regret and failure (ANN); the review notes psychological costs to the children of combat (to verify depth).
Teens with weapons as protagonists; the story frames it as a least-bad option rather than a model.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Arata answers threats to his children personally and with force.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Chain of command and discipline in his company; he left an employer's rules behind.

Civic vs kin.evidence: His adopted unit becomes family first (AniList review).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: A commander with devoted wards; earned rather than inherited rank.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Practical, tactical reasoning rather than custom guides choices.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival and money for the children's future dominate.

folkways.japan: An otaku protagonist finding purpose through group duty and paternal responsibility reflects Japanese themes of belonging and obligation to one's own.

delivery.evidence: ANN: volume 1 does not moralize and leaves judgment to readers; AniList reviewer says events are contrived to vindicate Arata.

personified.ideology: harm reduction: the least-bad option to protect one's own
profit at any cost, children as expendable

delivery.note: The series asks hard questions about war and child soldiers but, per one reviewer, arranges events so the hero's choices look justified.

winners_losers: Arata and his child soldiers win as an underdog family; exploitative profit-driven militarism loses sympathy, while the premise that arming the children is necessary goes largely unchallenged.
